We develop a semi-analytical model for dust growth in molecular clouds, focusing on low-metal content clouds. The model includes the breakup of parent grains during supernovae explosions and considers observations of dust temperatures in cloud cores. It also accounts for the growth of grains in a dynamic environment through the combination of supernovae explosions and stellar winds from massive stars. Our analysis of dust evolution in two specific solar-metallicity molecular clouds, W3(OH) and W51, shows that parent grain destruction during supernovae explosions is the dominant dust growth process. Furthermore, our model predicts the minimum mass required for a collapsing core to form a star and falls within the range predicted by observations and simulations of star formation. Additionally, our model confirms the importance of supernovae dust production, particularly in metal-poor environments. Our model also shows that dust growth through stellar winds of massive stars makes a negligible contribution to total dust mass. Our results have implications for the early formation of dust in the universe and the potential for dust to influence the formation of low-mass stars. Our model is applicable to any molecular cloud and can be used to study the formation of dust in different types of star-forming regions, such as giant molecular clouds. Detecting three-dimensional objects at a distance is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles, given that they may be required to react quickly to far-away objects. Unfortunately, existing three-dimensional detection methods typically struggle with such distances due to limited kinetic information and significant variations in object appearances under different viewing angles. This problem is particularly challenging for mid-to-far field objects, as their corresponding two-dimensional projections often overlap, making it difficult to establish a one-to-one correspondence between three-dimensional objects and their two-dimensional projections. To address this issue, we propose a novel distant three-dimensional detection framework far3det, which first utilizes feature extraction networks to obtain three-dimensional proposals through linear transformations, bypassing the mid-to-far field object-to-two-dimensional-projection challenge. far3det then refines these proposals using a non-linear regression module, ultimately producing accurate three-dimensional bounding boxes. To support extensive evaluation, we collect a far-field three-dimensional data set, demonstrate state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods, and show that our approach is efficient and effective for distant object detection. Furthermore, far3det exhibits practical potential for real-world applications. This research breakthrough is represented by a codebook available at https://github.com/leiming1991/far3det. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. However, estimating scene flow is complicated due to the presence of ambient features that can distract from calculating precise motion trajectories. Traditional approaches typically rely on surrounding features in the image for data-driven calculations but often get sidetracked by these distracting features instead of following the defined normals in the image. This particular issue is addressed by introducing a unique method of metric learning that encourages self-guided estimates of scene flow. This method uses two distinct metric learning techniques to evaluate the quality of both individual and joint predictions for scene flow. By conducting experiments on benchmark datasets under various conditions, this method demonstrates its capacity to enhance the accuracy of scene flow estimation. Notably, it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning baselines on the DTU dataset, achieving a mean relative error of 1.6, and also exhibits a 2-fold improvement in error compared to existing approaches on the EPICKENNEL dataset. This method's success indicates that using external features in the image for scene flow estimation is actually counterproductive. As a result, this method only uses intrinsic data from depth images, thereby avoiding the reliance on external features that often lead to erroneous predictions. This method's code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhai-kai/self-guided-scene-flow. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-aligned strange quark matter under an external magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Subsequently, we examine the structure of strange quark stars that assume spin-aligned condensates, accounting for the effects of temperature and magnetic field on their density, as well as the relation between the magnetic field and quark star's characteristics. Our model demonstrates that a critical temperature exists beneath the transition from deconfinement to the quark star phase. Additionally, both temperature and magnetic field were found to enhance the stability of spin-aligned strange quark stars. Our numerical simulations facilitate the derivation of equations describing the variation of strange quark star mass with temperature and magnetic intensity. We discovered that both increased temperature and magnetic field lead to expansions in the radius of the quark star, while the four-dimensional radius is proportional to the square of the magnetic intensity. Furthermore, the minimum mass and canonical mass of spin-aligned strange quark stars are found to be approximately 0.92 and 1.44 solar masses, respectively. These findings suggest that spin-aligned strange quark stars could possess diamagnetic properties, with a critical density located at the border between hadron and quark matter phases, dubbed the 'Hart' density. This 'Hart' density, approximately 7.92 times the Chandrasekhar limit, constitutes the maximum mass threshold for spin-aligned strange quark stars. Both temperature and magnetic field were found to enhance the magnetic moment of spin-aligned strange quark stars, leading to higher moment of inertia at increased temperatures and magnetic intensities. Our model also demonstrates that spin-aligned strange quark stars could exhibit superfluid properties, while temperature and magnetic field both contribute to an increase in their moment of inertia. Our derived equations facilitate the calculation of spin-aligned strange quark stars' physical properties, including their radius, volume, surface gravity, temperature, magnetic pressure, and chemical potential. We also explore the possibility of observing spin-aligned strange quark stars through X-ray radiation, revealing that temperature and magnetic field both play significant roles in the X-ray spectrum of these stars. Furthermore, the addition of magnetic field causes the separation of quark flavors, generating extra energy that, when released as X-ray radiation, enables the detection of spin-aligned strange quark stars at greater distances. This paper introduces a new concept called Timeloops, an automated system call filtering technique tailored for containerized microservices. Traditionally, system administrators rely on deny-all defaults for system call filtering, but this approach becomes impractical given the vast number of system calls and the frequency of code updates in modern microservice architectures. Our proposed method leverages a combination of static analysis and runtime data to create efficient system call filters that are uniquely optimized for each application deployment, eliminating the need for manual configuration and reducing the risk of security vulnerabilities. A prototype implementation of Timeloops was developed and tested using a variety of containerized applications, demonstrating its effectiveness and performance. The evaluation results show that Timeloops offers a viable solution for automated system call filtering in modern microservice environments. Furthermore, a security evaluation of the approach is conducted, and the source code of the implementation along with the evaluation methodology are available online for reference. As the frequency of remote interactions increases, the importance of secure temporary file storage also grows, a complementary project called Temploop that builds upon the Timeloops framework is introduced. The ultimate spatial resolution of Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs) is constrained by the partial coherence of the electron source and the microscope's optical system. To break this limit, the long-standing approach has been to employ optical instruments that manipulate the electron source's partial coherence. We propose a novel method where the programmable phase disk, initially introduced as a TEM image intensity modulator, is reconfigured to enforce a specific coherent transfer function (CTF) that compensates for optical system aberrations present in the TEM. By doing so, we demonstrate theoretically that it is possible to achieve high-resolution imaging by selecting the appropriate program for the disk, taking into account its discrete nature, foreign illumination, and the associated side lobes. The potential of this concept is illustrated through numerical simulation of a programmable phase disk in a TEM, showing that it is feasible to recover an object image even under conditions with significant side lobes. The scope of this idea is vast, given the variety of programming possible for the disk, thus making it a viable option to tackle various TEM imaging challenges. The proposed concept is amenable to implementation using the advanced electron optics found in latest-generation TEMs, thereby providing a feasible pathway to super-resolution in these microscopes. The potential of this approach to be extended to energy-filtered and ptychographic TEM imaging is also discussed. We outline the specifications for the programmable phase disk, highlighting the key parameters that this design must meet, including low thickness, minimal material loss, and the ability to modulate the electron intensity quickly enough to accommodate the varying coherence time of the electron source. The feasibility of fabricating a disk with these characteristics is demonstrated through the presentation of a prototype designed using a scanning electron microscope and a program called COMSOL, and we discuss the results of electron simulations using a full-field TEM simulator, including the recovery of a programmed disk's original pattern from the obtained image. Lastly, we outline a feasible pathway for implementing this concept in a TEM by designing an appropriate disk, transferring the required electronic controls, and finely tuning the microscope's optical system to match the selected disk's transfer function. The theoretical recovery of an object image in a TEM using a programmable phase disk sets the stage for the design of novel electron optics that can provide real-world super-resolution in these microscopes. We anticipate that this approach will pave the way for the development of a range of new transmission electron microscope technologies, including those for imaging biological specimens at high speed, as well as those requiring high-efficiency, high-resolution imaging in multiple directions

Determining the properties of M-dwarfs is crucial for many studies as these stars comprise roughly 75% of the stellar population in the galaxy. While M-dwarfs are typically found in binary or multiple star systems with luminous A, B, O, or blue-white K and G stars, there are countless instances of M-dwarfs in the field that don't have an associated companion of a specific brightness. Since M-dwarfs typically reside in the optical and near-infrared range, it's often difficult to obtain precise measurements of their basic characteristics through just one observation. To overcome this limitation, researchers developed a method of collecting UV spectra for M-dwarfs, utilizing data from the MARS survey. By leveraging spectra from 367 M-dwarfs, scientists developed a novel, empirical formula to calculate the surface temperature of these stars based on specific features in the UV spectrum. This new approach to determining the temperature of M-dwarfs was compared to traditional methods and was found to yield results with a similar level of accuracy. A new formula for estimating the stellar velocity was also presented, as well as a definition for the activity level of these stars. Ultimately, this new framework for collecting UV spectra of M-dwarfs will significantly enhance the accuracy of their parameter estimations, a critical step in utilizing these stars as lenses and microlenses, as well as in gravitational lensing events, and in the study of star-disc systems, among other areas of research. A new catalog of UV-collected spectra for M-dwarfs, along with their parameters, is also provided in this study and can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.5194/aasvol-2-1-2023 and will serve as a starting point for the larger M-dwarfs Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Collection (MUSIC) database, which will include optical and near-infrared data as well as UV spectra for 1500 M-dwarfs once complete. Researchers encourage all members of the astronomical community to contribute to this database, which has the potential to become the largest and most comprehensive collection of homogeneous M-dwarfs in the universe. A demonstration of the precision of these new measurements for a sample of 11 M-dwarfs found in the field of the BB King star, a multiple star system consisting of an A-type luminous companion and three M-dwarfs, is also provided, showing that the new measurements for these M-dwarfs are a significant improvement over their previous estimates. To address scalability issues with high-dimensional control systems, we've developed a second-order order achievable set computation method grounded in a modified Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation that incorporates a Cauchy-type term. This approach extends previous first-order strategies by utilizing a second-order Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enabling us to determine policy-dependent and independent achievable sets. Leveraging this method, we've derived a computational algorithm for evaluating closed-loop system performance and identifying required control objectives with a precision of $sqrt(epsilon)$, where $epsilon$ is a user-specified parameter. We've also demonstrated the effectiveness of this method through numerical examples. A correlation between the size of young star clusters and the age of these clusters has been observed in several galaxies.  To confirm the trend seen in previous studies, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of 2496 clusters in 19 galaxies using data from the Hubble Source Catalog.  Our results show that the relationship between cluster size and age holds true for a vast age range, extending from a few million years to around 10 billion years.  Additionally, we found that the slope of this correlation remains relatively constant across different galaxy types, which could indicate a universal physical process influencing the development of star clusters across various environments.  We also discovered a secondary branch of clusters with larger sizes at older ages, which we believe may be composed of clusters that formed in dust-rich environments or through the interaction of star clusters with their host galaxies.  To validate these findings, we performed a set of mock galaxy simulations using data from the IllustrisTNG100-000-000 dataset, which supported our cluster size-age analysis. Current deep learning techniques used in removing rain from images have achieved notable success. Nonetheless, the underlying mechanism of these models wasn't thoroughly explored. Our research delves into the core mathematics behind rain removal and, through a data-driven approach, uncovers the underlying distribution of rain from images. In doing so, we create a framework where rain is generated from clean images and vice versa. This framework enables not only rain removal but also the creation of realistic rain effects for filmmaking and video games. Our model's capabilities are showcased through comprehensive experiments on not only rain removal but also the generation of rain from images, with our results outperforming state-of-the-art competitors. The code for our model has been made publicly available on GitHub. In contrast to traditional methods, our approach produces rain effects that are realistic, adaptable to various scenarios, and efficiently handles multiple input images. Our research paves the way for the creation of high-realism rain effects in video games and the development of rain-free versions of videos taken in rainy conditions. The fact that rain generation and removal are inversely linked also opens up new avenues for the restoration of damaged images caused by rain. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the value of uncovering the underlying distribution of rain from images and the creation of rain effects through translation. This sets the stage for the exploration of more complex weather phenomena, such as cloud generation and removal, which is an area that our research initially tackles from a mathematical perspective. Moreover, the creation of realistic rain effects for filmmaking and video games can now be achieved at video resolutions of up to 4K. By leveraging next-generation computer vision capabilities, reward learning via observation of video data has become more feasible. However, determining an optimal policy using visual data can be challenging due to several issues, including the high cost of creating relevant data and the difficulty of effectively using raw visual information to predict rewards. To address these problems, we propose a pioneering framework that uses a combination of computer vision and machine learning to efficiently predict rewards from visual data. By first identifying clusters of similar states through vision-based comparisons, we significantly reduce the amount of visual data needed to train our reward model. We also introduce a novel learning algorithm that leverages feedback in the form of ranked clusters, which enables us to train state-action reward models at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. As a result, our approach allows us to develop efficient and accurate reward models that can be used to control a variety of tasks defined by visual data, even with limited actual experience of the task, and we demonstrate this with successful applications in control tasks. Furthermore, we showcase the generalization capabilities of our approach by successfully transferring knowledge from one variant of a task to another. We experimentally compare our method to multiple state-of-the-art baselines, and our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/author/carlfrico.2021.0032. Additionally, a video highlighting our approach's effectiveness in various scenarios is available at https://youtu.be/8Q9bQ4uL6fM. We successfully demonstrated our approach at IJCA special session on Visually Aided Machine Learning at MIR Labs, University at Buffalo, NY. In particular, we experimented with learning to complete a series of household tasks from scratch using just a few actual demonstrations, learning to navigate and collect virtual objects in a variety of environments, and efficiently learning to complete a series of surgical tasks using feedback in the form of ranked clusters of states. To overcome this limitation, we've developed ATOMIC, a comprehensive knowledge base that contains over half a million text samples describing diverse machine learning concepts. ATOMIC serves as an atlas, providing over 160 potential conclusions (or outcomes) that can be arrived at through simple if-then reasoning. In detail, ATOMIC encompasses 398 different machines or topics such as politics, sports, and entertainment, with each topic having its unique set of potential conclusions. To validate the utility of ATOMIC, we've created six different evaluation tasks that involve complex if-then reasoning and found that models trained on ATOMIC consistently outperformed those that were not trained on the atlas in our experiments. Notably, our findings showed that models trained on ATOMIC often developed biases that favored easy conclusions over more complex ones, posing a challenge for future researchers to mitigate this sort of bias through counterfactual learning. Nonetheless, ATOMIC offers a valuable resource for assessing a machine's ability to engage in complex if-then reasoning and its capacity to navigate diverse machine learning topics. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate that their conductivity can be modified through electromagnetic gates. To explain these observations in NbN, researchers propose the idea of coherent quantum phase-slips or Coulomb blockage to obstruct current flow. This paper aims to clarify the underlying mechanism by examining the conductivity of superconducting NbN nanowires in response to an adjacent electrical gate. To achieve this comprehension, the measurement setup involves two correlation transmission measurements that can be converted into each other. By doing so, this conversion enables the analysis of conductive state based on transmission measurements. In addition, accounting for backscattering allows for the understanding of phase-slips. However, the proposed model of quantum phase-slips faces a hurdle as the expected cross-sectional area based on fence-model of superconductivity is significantly larger than the actual nanowire dimension. Consequently, a blockage model emerges as a more plausible explanation for the observed conductivity phenomena. To validate this model, a method of measuring blockage voltage is established by utilizing a transmission measurement setup. The results show that the blockage voltage of NbN nanowires is around 3-4 times the superconducting gap voltage, consistent with the predicted values of 2-3 times in other materials with similar properties. Furthermore, a blockage model is applied to explain the behavior under different gate conditions, confirning that the model accurately accounts for the observed conductivity patterns. To take it a step further, the model is expanded to consider multiple blockage states, and a new approach is proposed to determine the specific blockage state based on the transmission coefficient. This expanded model provides a comprehensive understanding of the conductivity of superconducting NbN nanowires, offering a valuable framework for the design of nanoscale electronic devices. To facilitate replication of these findings, a detailed description of the measurement setup is outlined, and our results are further supported by a blockage model validation section. In conclusion, a comprehensive understanding of the conductivity of superconducting NbN nanowires is achieved by validating a Coulomb blockage model, which has significant implications for the design of blockage-based electronic devices. Furthermore, our study confirms that the average blockage voltage of NbN nanowires is approximately 3.5 times the superconducting gap voltage, providing a valuable reference point for blockage-based research. The APOLLO code's high accuracy in spectral data retrieval allows it to effectively handle a high degree of spectral fine structure, even when using a medium-resolution spectroscopy similar to that of the GENECHO instrument. We employed this code to reexamine GJ 229B, the first T-dwarf discovered in 1995, using high-resolution spectroscopy from the VLT FORS2. The newly acquired data, along with the code's retrievals from lower-resolution VLT FXE spectra, enable a more comprehensive analysis of GJ 229B's atmospheric characteristics. This analysis uncovered evidence of molecular absorption features in water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, methane, ammonia, and phosphine. However, the presence of these molecules varies depending on the analysis method employed. While the code's results from the higher-resolution FORS2 spectroscopy and the higher signal-to-noise ratio FXE spectra correspond reasonably well, the assignment of CO and CH4 based on the FXE data may be questionable due to the smaller size of the absorption features, which could be consistent with a healthier methane abundance. Notably, both analysis methods pinpoint a temperature below 1,300 K, a surface gravity of around 10 bar, and a CH4 pressure around 2 bar. Nevertheless, the code's outcomes highlight the difficulty in obtaining a precise picture of this distant world's properties and suggest that further, higher-resolution and higher signal-to-noise data are necessary to refine our understanding of GJ 229B. Additionally, the code's results on this target, the first of its kind, hold significant implications for the numerous T-dwarfs that have been identified more recently. construction by Cramer and Shoumakhov in 2004 as an example. Subsequent work by
Hohenberger and Waters in 2009 further developed this framework, and it has since
been referred to as the CHHW framework. Over time, the term "unforgeable encryption"
has become associated with this framework. This paper re-examines the terminology
and associated security goals within the context of modern cryptography, ultimately
proposing revised definitions for unforgeable encryption that address previous
weaknesses and considerations. Additionally, this paper presents novel proofs
for unforgeable encryption constructions, while also exploring relationships
between unforgeable encryption and other cryptographic security goals. Finally,
this paper raises new research questions and considerations for unforgeable
encryption. Moreover, this paper proposes a new framework for public-key encryption
with public key exposure, referred to as the UFE-CCA-SE framework, along with
unforgeable encryption being redefined as a form of this framework. This new
definition is then applied to a well-known construction, and this application
yields a novel consideration regarding public-key attacks. Ultimately, this paper
raises two primary research questions for future investigation. Firstly, it seeks to
confirm whether its revised definition for unforgeable encryption is inherently
stronger than the original definition, particularly in relation to adaptively
secure public-key encryption. Secondly, it seeks to investigate whether its new
UE-CCA-SE framework can be achieved by a specific construction that originally
yielded an unforgeable encryption scheme, according to the CHHW framework. This
paper provides theoretical proof and a proposed construction for achieving a
public-key encryption scheme that is both unforgeable and secure against leakage,
but this construction is for a specific form of leakage and only yields a
construction for a system with an increased key size. This paper hopes to spark
further discussion on the future of unforgeable encryption, while also raising
considerations for future work in this area. Unforgeable encryption continues to

Unlike the results from our dry experiments, those with high water content showed a more significant decrease in friction when temperatures rose, eventually becoming as low as 10% of their initial value at 600K. This significant drop could have a notable impact on planetary growth, potentially allowing particles to move more freely at higher temperatures and contributing to the formation of larger particles seen in some laboratory experiments and planetary systems. Our research demonstrates efficient and effective learning of complex tasks with minimal reliance on precise reinforcement learning signals, facilitating future exploration of our EKMP framework in various contexts. By sharing our research findings with the broader community, we also reveal that our EKMP framework can be used to enhance robotic learning for sensitive environments that require fast adaptation, such as operating rooms where cross-contamination is a concern. The Southern Atlantic Ridge system forms the boundary between Africa and South America, and within this boundary there is a notable offset in the mid-ocean ridge, commonly referred to as the South Atlantic fracture zone.  Offshore of Brazil, this fracture zone extends approximately 2,500 kilometers in length and displays unique characteristics where deep-sea valleys narrow down to near-requisites at their western and eastern ends.  Research indicates that these features are the result of ridge-parallel shifts along the S.A. fracture zone.  Modeling of this movement shows that the axis of the Brazilian deep-sea valleys is being pulled apart at a rate of 1-2 centimeters per year, and modeling of the East Brazilian deep-sea lows indicates that they are being pulled apart at a significantly faster rate of 10-20 centimeters per year.  This research also found that non-seismic methods can be utilized to study the kinematics and morphology of deep-sea fracture zones.  This utilization involved analyzing bathymetric charts and backscatter data from sub-bottom profiles, combining this with magnetic anomaly data in order to gain insight into the structure and development of these unique features.  We propose that the E.B. deep-sea lows be added to the list of absolute time scales in the South Atlantic, with a starting time of 31.5 million years ago, and also propose that the axis of the Brazilian deep-sea valleys serve as a relative time scale with a starting time of 34 million years ago.  Modeling of this data puts forth the idea that the S.A. ridge system began shifting in the Eocene, and modeling of modeling indicates that the Brazilian and African sides of the ridge system began shifting in the Oligocene.  We also found that the time it takes for the S.A. ridge system to complete one full cycle of shifting is approximately 30-40 million years. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functional properties is not yet fully understood, but it's believed that the spatial arrangement of knots could affect protein flexibility and stability. To investigate this hypothesis, a computational model was developed to analyze the topological structure of L-knots in air and their reflections in water, based on molecular dynamics simulations. By examining 200 randomly generated L-knots in vacuum and their corresponding structures in water, the model identified relationships between the spatial arrangement of L-knots and their reflection in water. Specifically, it found that certain spatial arrangements could prevent proteins from flexibly adapting to their surrounding environment, potentially impacting their stability. To further explore this concept, the model was applied to the structural data of real knotted proteins, analyzing their native states and predicted configurations in water through visualizations and computational measurements of flexibility. The results showed that some real proteins with L-knots in their native state may have limited flexibility due to the spatial arrangement of their knots, and that a topological analysis of these structures could provide valuable insights into protein function and evolution. Moreover, this approach was discovered to be highly robust, making it an useful tool for the growing field of topological biochemistry. By incorporating this model into a web server and database designed to analyze the spatial arrangement of L-knots in proteins, it's now possible to predict the functional consequences of these structures, information that could be utilized by life scientists and the general public in searching for functional relationships in proteins with complex structures. This tool allows users to explore the relationship between the spatial arrangement of L-knots and protein function, and it includes a detailed guide on how to use it, along with a series of educational videos on YouTube. Additionally, a educational course on topological biochemistry has been developed, and it's being offered as a special topic in graduate programs in chemistry and biology. This model and the resources provided are available at https://knop.top/ and https://db.knop.top/. Current techniques can readily generate text based on given input, but when asked to produce alternative scenarios, they struggle. These statements differ in at least one phrasal element, such as 'The book was not interesting' versus 'The movie was not interesting'. To achieve this, we adapted a contrastive learning algorithm and fine-tuned pre-trained language models for counterfactual tasks. Our findings demonstrate that large language models perform satisfactorily on this task and showcase the potential of our DISCO dataset to advance counterfactual understanding among NLP models. Furthermore, our results underscore the significance of releasing datasets in the form of counterfactual pairs, as this enables the development of more versatile and adaptive models capable of producing diverse output given the same input context. Precise and near-real-time flood forecasting is crucial for saving lives and minimizing financial losses. However, achieving this requires the rapid solution of fluid dynamics equations that can be challenging even for traditional numerical methods. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that uses deep learning to quickly solve the shallow water equations across various flood scenarios, yielding highly accurate results. By leveraging a massive dataset of buoyant fluids compiled through extensive SPH simulations, we developed a convolutional neural network that can predict water heights with just a few milliseconds. Our model's performance is showcased across five distinct flood scenarios, including when obstacles are present, where it demonstrates an impressive mean absolute error of less than one centimeter when compared to the results of extensive SPH simulations. Furthermore, we explore the influence of incorporating turbulence into the shallow water equations on flood forecasting and propose a new framework for rapid flood simulation using multiple models. This framework enables us to generate diverse buoyant fluid scenarios, enabling us to create a massive dataset of 512 million buoyant fluid simulations through a distributed deep learning process. In addition to flood forecasting, our approach can also be applied to other fluid-based scenarios. In partnership with the Met Office, we aim to integrate this rapid flood forecasting model with real-time weather data to provide critical near-real-time flood warnings. Our open-source code is available on GitHub, where we invite the broader scientific community to explore and contribute to our research. A comprehensive understanding of heat distribution within an industrial fluidized bed is crucial for enhancing the efficiency and uniformity of the process.  Despite numerous studies, a key obstacle remains in achieving this understanding due to the lack of suitable measurement techniques that can rapidly and accurately assess temperature fluctuations within this type of system.  A novel method utilizing a temperature-sensitive NMR scan was developed to measure temperature within a gas-solid fluidized bed, allowing for the collection of temperature data at a rate of 10 Hz.  A carrier gas flow was used to supply air flow into the bed, and the effects of varying parameters such as bed size, solid flow rate, and heat input were studied using this method.  The data collected showed that increasing the size of the bed or the rate at which solids are added results in a greater variation in temperature, whereas increasing heat input has the opposite effect.  Furthermore, two distinct regimes were identified in the bed: a lower bed region with temperature fluctuations similar to those in a stationary solid layer, and an upper bed region with temperature fluctuations more than double as great as the lower bed region.  The data collected using this method will be useful in validating models of heat distribution within fluidized beds and in further research aimed at optimizing the operation of these systems.  In addition, this method may be adapted for use in other types of fluidized and fluid flow systems.  A bed of approximately 300 milliliters in size was used in the research described here, and it is believed that the method will also be effective with larger beds, provided that the NMR scan can be modified to collect data quickly enough. This field's primary objective is to create realistic video content that convinces viewers, which has numerous practical applications in entertainment, education, and marketing fields. This survey delves into the evolution of convincing video generation techniques, starting from early approaches using hand-animated data and progressing through the use of neural networks for data manipulation. We also discuss the current shortage of high-quality datasets available for training neural models and the importance of developing more versatile evaluation methods that can assess a model's performance in creating convincing videos from start to finish. We hope this survey will serve as a valuable resource for academics and practitioners working in this field and contribute to the advancement of convincing video generation technology. Hitherto, fabrication constraints have limited applications to visible wavelengths exceeding 100 $\mu$m. We overcome these boundaries by developing a technique for ultrathin microacoustic metamaterials utilizing two-photon polymerization. Our model incorporates a spatially periodic structure composed of rod elements oriented perpendicular to each other and equivalent in length to half the wavelength of operation. A powerful control design framework is introduced, allowing the creation of control systems from informal, conversational specifications written in a simple, first-order logic-based language. This language includes common phrases such as "the system should stay close to the target when it's close enough," "the system should move towards the target at a decreasing rate when it's too far away," and "the system should maintain a desired pattern when it's close enough." It's proven that any conversationally-specified system of the desired form exists, using a novel method that involves translating the conversational language into a set of continuous, differential inclusions, and then using a type of Lyapunov function to show that the resulting system meets the specified conditions. This approach makes it possible to find a suitable control strategy for systems with unbounded controls, which is demonstrated through an example involving the regulation of a pendulum swinging above its pivot point. This research is a follow-up to the work presented in https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12842, with additional contributions including a new method for translating the conversational language into a set of continuous differential inclusions, and a more flexible framework for proving the existence of a Lyapunov function using a descent price method. This new framework is then applied to a shooting method for solving boundary value problems, which is a key component in the control of systems with unbounded controls. In the context of Assured Safety and Security, addressing uncertainty from unknown or unaccounted events is a major issue due to the limitless nature of possibilities outside of their scope. The current approaches to handling uncertainty, such as using coverage metrics or probabilistic models with fixed distributions, fall short as they cannot capture the implications of open-world uncertainty and cannot be efficiently updated with the arrival of new information. This paper presents a novel uncertainty model based on energy forms that can efficiently handle such situations by providing a way to calculate the impact of all scenarios, regardless of their specificity. This model can be updated with new information by transforming the calculation into an optimization problem, making it suitable for use in learning algorithms. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this model through a prototype application involving the learning of a kinetic energy model, and show that it can be used to calculate safe ranges for uncertain values in real-time. This model has the potential to be adapted for use in other learning contexts. The model's source code is available for public use. We also discuss future directions for the development of uncertainty models in scenarios involving open-world settings. A key aspect for future research in this field should be the exploration of alternative ways to define energy forms that can be adapted to specific applications, as well as developing new computational tools to transform learning algorithms into assurable forms. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation environments that can assess a model's generalization capabilities as it learns in a lifelong learning framework. To address this need, we present L2Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation environment that allows for the continuous evaluation of lifelong learning strategies in complex exploration-driven tasks. L2Explorer is designed to simulate an infinite stream of randomized reinforcement learning tasks, enabling us to conduct comprehensive, controlled experiments to investigate how well a given method generalizes when confronted with an endless array of unfamiliar tasks. The performance of our proposed method, a novel variation of meta reinforcement learning, is evaluated in depth using L2Explorer in the context of generalization across different tasks. The underlying architecture of L2Explorer is an open-source collection of challenging exploration tasks set within realistic simulation environments, and it is easy to extend to support additional domains and evaluation scenarios. The code for L2Explorer, along with your action-oriented evaluation framework known as ActEval, can be downloaded from https://github.com/christopherumenberg/ActEval, making it possible for you to conduct your own thorough evaluation of life-long reinforcement learning strategies. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SMD) allows for the transmission of multiple modes through a single optical channel, potentially surpassing this restriction. In a two-photon system, SMD is achieved through the correlation of two photons' spatial properties following a nonlinear interaction. While this approach has been theoretically idealized with no additional resolution constraints, our analysis reveals that real-world applications are constrained by the size of the collected field and are therefore dependent on the specific setup. We propose a method to circumvent these constraints by employing a metamaterial lens in a two-photon SMD system, enabling transmission of high-frequency spatial modes with only a fraction of the typical intensity, contrary to previous methods that require extensive intensity enhancement. Through simulation, we demonstrate that this approach can overcome the Rayleigh criterion limitation for intensity measurements in the far field. Furthermore, we explore the application of this method to the transmission of high-spectral-bandwidth optical signals, a capability we refer to as super-resolution transmission. We analyze various potential constraints and identify the quantum nature of the transmitted photons as the most limiting factor in this process. We estimate the proposed method's potential for improving super-resolution transmission beyond the Rayleigh criterion in idealized scenarios but also consider the constraints imposed by real-world components, which could further limit the approach's effectiveness. To better grasp cross-cultural sentiment, sentiment analysis must be able to operate across languages. Nonetheless, sentiment datasets in other languages are often scarce. A common multi-task learning approach, where models are trained on multiple related tasks, can be effective for learning essential skills from limited labeled data. We believe that learning to analyze sentiment in one language can also be beneficial for analyzing sentiment in other languages, provided those languages share similarities such as script or geography. To test this hypothesis, we created datasets for fine-grained sentiment analysis in Hindi and performed a series of experiments to evaluate the benefits of multi-task learning. Our findings show that pre-training on English yields more impressive results than pre-training on Hindi, which may be attributed to the larger size of the English dataset. Notably, our best-performing model was one that was pre-trained on both English and Hindi for sentiment classification before being adapted to analyze Hindi from different visual cues. This confirms our hypothesis and highlights the significance of comparative studies in evaluating the benefits of cross-lingual multi-task learning. A key tool for safeguarding this confidentiality is employee-assisted decryption, a process where an encrypted message is transformed back into plain text with the help of the original sender. It has numerous applications, including those in end-to-end encryption and secure multi-party computation. A notable example is PGP, still widely used for encrypting emails by individuals and corporations alike. A notable aspect of this process is that it permits the state to force an individual to decrypt a particular file. This phenomenon may seem surprising, given typical views on coercion and encryption. To address this concern, we introduce a new class of coercion attacks, distinct from both key extraction and decryption attacks. A crucial discovery made in this research is that the privacy of encrypted data can be safeguarded against any attacker, including the state, as long as the original sender is trustworthy. This conclusion holds true regardless of whether the system in place is considered healthy or vulnerable to key-related attacks. Furthermore, we outline a method to enhance programs that employ decryption, as well as encryption, to prevent any coercion that could compromise confidentiality. This new framework for programs that employ both forms of security is then applied to PGP in an email context. The outcome of this application is a new, state-induced coercion attack class, along with an analysis of the underlying principles and the mechanics of PGP. Lastly, we investigate the principles of program fairness and user experience, in addition to security, and show that PGP, reinforced with our new attack class, represents the ideal solution for balancing these considerations. In recent years, deep neural networks have excelled at solving complex, real-world pattern recognition problems across various fields, yet their performance is largely unexplained. Comprehending their internal workings and decision-making processes is crucial for addressing potential biases, ensuring reliability in sensitive areas, and providing essential context for deploying AI-powered solutions. Unfortunately, current research has yielded few methods that can effectively interpret the behavior of these complex models. This study offers a practical, yet theoretical approach to developing a deeper understanding of deep neural networks by focusing on three key aspects: (1) network structure and parameter significance, (2) data visualization to reveal key features, and (3) qualitative explanations of predictive decisions. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach by applying it to two popular deep learning frameworks, specifically Inception V4 and Residual Network (RN). We also provide initial insights into the behavior and decision-making processes of these models, as well as the complementary methods for their interpretation. Furthermore, we make our model and this interpretation framework widely available for further exploration and improvement. The Group Lasso is a well-known technique for reducing model complexity in high-dimensional feature spaces by eliminating entire groups of unimportant variables. Nonetheless, selecting groups a priori can be challenging, if not impossible, when dealing with complex data structures such as those encountered in genetics, microarray analysis, or sociology. This study introduces an iterative method that refines and relaxes constraints to facilitate sparse modeling within groups, thereby enabling the Group Lasso to effectively handle real-valued, nominal, and ordinal data variables. The new approach is called the Iterative Group Lasso, and we establish theoretical convergence results and a suitable optimization strategy. Moreover, we demonstrate through extensive simulations that the Iterate soft-thresholding method achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we apply the Iterative Group Lasso to actual and simulated data sets, showcasing its capability for handling complex variables and achieving sparsity. The proposed method is implemented in the R package IterGroupLasso, freely available for download. Ultimately, we explore possible extensions to other sparsity-promoting techniques.

Our team used the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for spatially resolved, optical emission line observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With data from multiple optical emission lines, we calculated key physical properties such as oxygen abundance, star formation rate, and gas mass. Our findings from initial data analyses for 9 targets are as follows: At 10 sigma confidence, we detected 10+log(O/H) with a precision of 0.05 on average and identified 7 objects as showing evidence of star formation. SFR calculations yielded values ranging from 10 to 1000.2 in units of Solar Masses per year. Finally, our estimated mass range for the 9 U/LIRGs was 10^10.4 to 10^12.3, covering nearly 3 logarithmic mass units. These outcomes demonstrate the capabilities of the KOOLS-IFU and Seimei Telescope for exploring gas physics within a specific and diverse sample of galaxies. Further data analysis will provide a more comprehensive understanding of these galaxies' physical properties and phenomena such as starburst and AGN activity across various stages of galaxy merger processes. A preliminary analysis of our data suggests a need for further studies on individual objects like GOALS-033, which showed unusually low oxygen abundance among its multiple components or objects like GOALS-083, whose high gas mass relative to star formation indicates a galaxy in search of its host mass. These data also are available at the KOOLS-IFU database available at https://db.astro.seimei.ac.jp/koools_ifu/. Based on these outcomes, our team believes that the KOOLS-IFU and Seimei Telescope will be an effective and powerful instrument for uncovering the physics of gas and gas interacting with its host star in various types of galaxies across various distances up to z = 0.2. We investigate the changes in entanglement and synchronization for two-qubit states represented in their respective tomograms. A new measure for states' similarity is proposed, based on the variance of their marginal probabilitiy distributions. This method enables us to locally identify the initial stages of states' synchronization and entanglement change directly from their tomographic data. Specifically, we demonstrate that increasing entanglement in a Mach-Zehnder-like interferometer leads to a decrease in the proposed similarity measure, while a qubit's partial decoupling from another qubit results in an increase in this measure before the state becomes unentangled. Furthermore, we show that there is a direct correlation between this similarity measure and another established measure of states' similarity, the Hilbert-Schmidt distance. This analysis has significant implications for state tomography, given that it may be possible to infer changes in an state's entanglement or synchronization simply by analyzing its tomographic data. This is especially relevant when considering the complexity of performing actual measurements on these states, as it would provide a more indirect yet still meaningful way of determining these changes. A key aspect of crop production is controlling plant diseases through accurate forecasting and effective treatment. For the strawberry disease, crown rot, caused by Fusarium oxysporum, precise prediction and treatment are crucial as the disease spreads quickly and affects the entire crop. In the past, researchers proposed several methods for managing this disease; however, they lacked a standardized comparison. Our study creates a framework to evaluate these methods and applies it to the specific problem of managing crown rot in strawberries. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for real-time data processing. Due to its growing popularity, it's essential to develop effective methods for detecting and repairing data inconsistencies. As such, we've developed a transactional integrity validation and repair system for MongoDB, leveraging existing techniques and adapting them to account for MongoDB's TPC-C and YCSB workloads. A key innovation in our approach is the use of a finite state automaton to efficiently validate transactional integrity, while repair strategies are divided into two methods: a conflict-resolution technique and a log-based approach. We've evaluated our system, incorporating a state-machine-based validation method and a repair method, and found it to be more efficient than other alternatives. Furthermore, we've conducted a comparative analysis of our system's performance, observing that MongoDB's TPC-C performance is significantly impacted by the introduction of our system, while YCSB performance is less affected. Additionally, we've explored the state machine's behavior under different data sets and observed that MongoDB's YCSB workloads tend to produce state machines with fixed numbers of states. We've released an open-source implementation of our system, along with a custom TPC-C test suite tailored for embedded document data. Overall, we've demonstrated the feasibility of validating transactional integrity in MongoDB. Speech emotion recognition is a complex task due to varying data availability across different domains, intense feature learning requirements, and the need for sophisticated models to achieve satisfactory performance. Experimental evaluations conducted on the SpeechEmo-3000 dataset demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, a key aspect of this study involves providing a technical overview of deep reinforcement learning techniques that can guide other researchers in similar transfer learning scenarios. The unrolling of an adhesive tape exhibits a complex and unpredictable sound pattern as it occurs, commonly characterized as a crackling noise.  This study reveals that the acoustic waveform exhibits a highly organized structure, comprising repetitive patterns that are derived from the sudden release of stored energy as the tape unwinds. A mathematical model is developed to illustrate how these patterns emerge, specifically showing how the curvature of the tape influences the formation of specific sound frequencies. Through both analytical modeling and experimental data, evidence is presented to support the existence of concealed order within the seemingly random sound produced by an unwinding adhesive tape. This research has implications for enhancing the precision of sensors that rely on the sound produced by unwinding tapes, as well as for improving the performance of pressure sensors fabricated using unwinding tape sensors. Additionally, this study demonstrates a novel approach to manufacturing concealed periodic structures within tape sensors, thereby enabling the detection of irregular pressures. Furthermore, this study is relevant to the development of advanced techniques for analyzing complex sounds within physiological contexts, such as the sounds associated with swallowing or heartbeats. This method is applied to the analysis of acoustic waveform data obtained from the unrolling of adhesive tapes, as well as the electrocardiogram data associated with the heartbeats of human subjects. A distinct pattern is discovered using this integrated approach, referred to as a "rosetta pattern," which provides a more comprehensive understanding of the unrolling of adhesive tapes, as well as the rhythmic patterns present within heartbeats. A new perspective on the concept of order and disorder is presented, emphasizing the significance of a disordered state in both biological and non-biological systems, as well as the importance of the "order parameter," which serves as a measure of disorder. We investigate the process of material homogenization, focusing on a composite material with a high-contrast microstructure that consists of densely connected conductive inclusions set within a nonconducting matrix. The homogenization process is examined under two conditions: when the inclusions have a complex geometry and when the inclusions are differential. Notably, our study relaxes a typical assumption found in homogenization theory. For a differential inclusion with a smooth boundary, we prove that when the inclusions are small enough, their effect on a given function can be approximated by a specific linear transformation. This analysis extends to vector-valued functions and provides a corresponding result for differential inclusions with non-smooth boundaries, demonstrating the occurrence of material homogenization through a different approach. These findings are applicable to the study of conductive composite materials. Additionally, we explore the possibility of replacing the differential inclusion with a suitable limit of torus-shaped inclusions, which has implications for the study of elliptic and parabolic differential equations within the context of homogenization. Our work is also relevant to the examination of quasilinear and nonlinear differential equations, including those arising in the study of composite materials. A notable result concerning a quasilinear differential equation leads to a corresponding theorem for a nonlinear differential equation, providing a path forward in the study of homogenization within a broader context. These theorems on homogenization are established under conditions that are weaker than those typically required in homogenization theory. Our work lays a foundation for further investigation into the process of material homogenization, encompassing a broader examination of a differential inclusion and its impact on both smooth and non-smooth boundary geometry. Nonetheless, our research is centered on a specific composite material and its resulting differential effects, which give rise to distinct mathematical outcomes, including those derived from a limit analysis that considers a filling curve with a varying diameter. These outcomes demonstrate the occurrence of material homogenization, expressing it as a differential operation that can be a rotation, reflection, or a combination of both, depending on the specific geometry of the filling curve. This resulting differential operation defines the outcome of the homogenization process in a corresponding limit analysis, providing a comprehensive understanding of the process of material homogenization that occurs when a nonconducting matrix contains densely connected conductive inclusions. This knowledge of material homogenization is valuable in estimating the behavior of physical quantities that satisfy a given differential equation, such as the flow of an electric current within a composite material. We establish a new criterion for the $\varepsilon$-isometric basis property in finite-dimensional $\ell_p$ spaces, where $0 < p \le 2$. Specifically, we show that given any subset $A$ of the unit ball in $\ell_p$, a basis $\Phi$ for the span of $A$ is $\varepsilon$-isometric if and only if the series representation of elements in $\lambda A$ is unique for almost every $\lambda$ in $\Delta_p^n$, a set of measure $1-\varepsilon$ on the unit ball in the dual space of $\ell_p^n$. This equivalence holds for bases in the span of unit vectors in $\ell_p$. We also demonstrate that in the case of Banach spaces, isomorphism (or $\varepsilon$-isomorphism) of finite-dimensional subspaces is not a transitive property. Furthermore, we prove that any finite-dimensional subspace of a Banach space with a Schauder basis admits a basis that induces an $\varepsilon$-isometric dimension increase. Finally, we establish that in the unit ball of any finite-dimensional $\ell_p$ space, there exist strongly independent vectors with an $\varepsilon$-isometric basis property. Additionally, we show that in the unit ball of any finite-dimensional $\ell_1$ space, there exist strongly independent vectors with an isometric basis property. Lastly, we demonstrate that in the unit ball of any finite-dimensional $\ell_\infty$ space, there exist strongly independent vectors with a basis that induces an $\varepsilon$-isometric dimension increase. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. As experiments reach high sensitivity, instrumental systematic errors become a major limitation in extracting information from data. To bridge the gap between theoretical instrument models and actual data analysis procedures, researchers need accessible and realistic simulations of instrument effects. To meet this need, we present the s4cmb toolkit, enabling users to generate realistic simulations of cosmic microwave background experiments that incorporate instrumental systematic errors in signal, polarization, and spatial dimensions. By utilizing this tool, we investigate the impact of instrumental systematic errors on two current experiments, CMB-S4 and Advanced ACT, using their respective design specifications. Our analysis confirms that the s4cmb toolkit accurately simulates instrument effects and reveals that the tool can be adapted to analyze the effects of instrumental systematic errors on any current or future CMB experiments. As such, we believe s4cmb will prove a valuable resource for researchers, statisticians, and instrument scientists working in the field of cosmic microwave background research. By utilizing this tool, we also demonstrate its utility in evaluating the performance of custom instrument configurations, a capability that will be particularly beneficial as future CMB experiments undergo design optimization during the design phase. Our analysis suggests that their performance is often dependent on their ability to reorder words in a meaningful way. We investigated the capabilities of a specific type of pre-trained language model, a transformer-based model like BART, in a simple word arrangement task without additional context. Our experiments showed that BART's strengths lie in arranging small groups of words, but its performance deteriorates as the size of the group increases. We discovered that using multiple sentences as input significantly improves BART's performance, allowing it to arrange up to seven words correctly. We found that BART's word order preferences are influenced by its statistical biases rather than any underlying grammatical rules. We also found that BART's arrangements often resemble the original input order or create semantically equivalent orderings. We observed a gap between BART's ability to arrange words in isolation versus in conjunction with other words. We discovered that some words are more easily arranged than others, with abstract concepts being more difficult to arrange than concrete ones. We found that the order of words can impact the understanding of their meaning, which we demonstrated through an additional experiment on sentence comprehension. We found a negative correlation between BART's word arrangement accuracy and its comprehension accuracy. We discovered that high-quality word arrangements are rare, which we validated through an additional unsupervised evaluation. We used this metric to compare BART to a language model fine-tuned for word arrangement, which we found performed better at every level of difficulty. In this research, we explore the performance of randomly generated low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes that have a specific degree distribution characteristic, where the degrees of the codeword bits are closely matched. To analyze this, we develop an analytical model that utilizes an exchange process to describe the behavior of LDPC encoders and decoders. Our analysis indicates that the degree-related LDPC codes exhibit better resistance to error decoding than traditional LDPC codes. We further demonstrate that the improved performance of these codes can be achieved in the context of binary erasure channels. Additionally, we derive the parameters of degree-related LDPC codes that achieve the maximum fusion threshold and provide a code design framework with enhanced decoding capabilities. Researchers examine the phenomenon of charge generation in metals when exposed to neutral shockwaves, specifically focusing on the impact of oblique shockwaves on copper samples.  An experiment is detailed where a normal shock generated by a loudspeaker was directed at a copper plate using water as a medium.  Measurements showed that the resulting electric current varied based on the orientation of the plate with peaks occurring when aligned with the direction of the shock's propagation.  This behavior is attributed to the movement of the shock's leading edge and its interaction with the plate's surface.  A proposed model suggests that the observed current fluctuations arise from the modulation of the shock's leading edge as it interacts with the plate, leading to varying electron speeds and resulting electric current.  This model was validated through additional experiments, including those involving optical measurements and the use of a flat water surface to generate a Mach reflection.  These experiments demonstrated that the critical factor influencing the electric current is not the velocity of the shock but rather the velocity of the precursor wave.  A key finding of this research is that the electric current exhibited a greater response to changes in the precursor wave velocity than to changes in shock velocity, underscoring the importance of precursor waves in the charge generation process.  A potential application of this phenomenon in the creation of a new type of sensor is also explored.  While the discovered relationship between the electric current and the orientation of the shockwave holds promise for developing a sensing method, further work is needed to fully explore and perfect this approach.  One potential avenue for optimization might involve a different metal with a higher charge response to the shockwave than copper. Instead, this research centers on leveraging this phenomenon to create a sensing mechanism that could be sensitive to minor changes in a shockwave's direction.  A key advantage of this sensing approach would be its ability to function in both gas and liquid environments over short to extended distances. Building on preimage functors for representations, we establish a cluster character formula for affine and finite simple Lie algebras. This connects morphisms of quantized semi-simple Lie algebras to cluster characters of their representations, extending work by Hernandez and M\'endez in type A. Moreover, this framework enables us to determine the character of a module by analyzing its preimage under the algebra's deformation functor, particularly when this module is irreducible in the Ginzburg resolution. As a result, we derive character formulas for irreducible representations of quantum groups, their superversions, and U_q(POS)_c, extending previous works by Kashiwara, Nakajima, Lusztig, Hernandez, M\'endez, and others. Our approach also facilitates the computation of character tables for finite quantum groups and their superversions. Lastly, we find that the Frobenius-Perron eigencharacter of the algebra under the deformation functor corresponds to the center of the algebra in a rational domain. Additionally, we establish isomorphisms between twisted Yangians, quantum algebras, and their superversions, using the preimage functors and cluster characters. This is reflected in the characters of these algebras and their modules, providing a new perspective on the representation theory of quantum groups and their subalgebras. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this framework to other Lie algebras and superalgebras. As a reference, we include a detailed character table for the Lie algebra of type D_4(1). The performance of the optimized lessons relies on the diversity of the students' interactions. For decentralized learning settings, where agents collaborate in a network, we introduce the concept of distributionally robust decentralized teaching, involving the creation of learning mechanisms that can adapt to changes in the agents' collaborative distribution. We develop the DR-DSGD algorithm to minimize the educational cost by formulating a semidefinite program that considers a wide range of collaborative scenarios. Our theoretical analysis shows that DR-DSGD yields an approximately optimal solution and is suitable for large-scale problems. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of DR-DSGD through comprehensive experiments in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Our results indicate that DR-DSGD is highly efficient and remarkably robust in handling a wide range of possible collaborative scenarios. We also find that our proposed algorithm is particularly effective in promoting diversity in settings with a large number of agents. We examine the measurement of the phase in quantum systems with the example of tight-binding models representing light-matter interactions in photonic environments. A comparative analysis is made between different measures of the phase, specifically the Feynman phase, geometric phase, and Wannier phase. It is shown that these measures yield distinct results when calculated using different many-body wave function representations. A consistent geometric phase can only be achieved when considering complete sets of measurement operators, derived from Wannier functions. A protocol is outlined for the consistent determination of the geometric phase in periodic systems from first-principle tight-binding models. Our study is relevant to the evaluation of quantum systems subject to continuous measurement, as is the case with systems undergoing rapid scanning in optical near-field spectroscopy. We also highlight the importance of distinguishing between different phase measures, particularly in the interpretation of experimental results. Clouds with inconsistencies can hinder performance, thus it is essential to develop efficient techniques for smoothing such data sets. Prior research has revealed that a single flawed data point can significantly impact the overall precision of estimators used for task execution, such as navigation, optical flow, and detection. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method, called Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC), which leverages unique transformation properties of 3D points to smooth data sets. TPC is characterized by three key components that enable it to achieve exceptional performance. Firstly, TPC employs a unique transformation-based filtering mechanism that flushes out inconsistent data points. Secondly, it utilizes a thin plate model that smoothes data sets while preserving geometric properties. Thirdly, TPC develops a flip-invariant smoothing algorithm tailored to point clouds, which improves the accuracy of estimators in autonomous systems. We're investigating medium access control (MAC) protocols for generate code waveforms (GCFW) radar networks that utilize frequency modulation continuous wave (FMCW) technology. We develop an analytical framework to study the performance of ALOHA and CSMA protocols in the presence of interference, and compared their results to a ideal, centralized scheduling method. A specific scenario is considered where radar devices operate in an ad-hoc mode and there are up to $N$ devices within range of the main radar system. A Slotted ALOWA protocol is modeled such that a radar device can transmit once per data frame period, and there is no restriction on interfering with other devices during this time. In contrast, the CSMA protocol prevents devices from transmitting if they detect the presence of another transmitting device, assuming detection occurs the entire data frame period. In terms of throughput, the ALOHA protocol achieves a throughput of $\frac{1}{N}$ when there are $N$ devices, the CSMA protocol results in no transmission occurring when there are more than two devices, and the ideal scheduling method allows for maximum throughput of one-time transmission event among all devices. A practical, modified CSMA protocol is also proposed to dynamically adjust to changing environments and manage interference more effectively. This protocol utilizes feedback in the form of interference patterns that can be obtained from receiving devices, enabling it to determine the best course of action and improve throughput in the face of competing radar systems. This protocol is shown to perform similarly to the ideal scheduling method, especially in scenarios where the data frame period is significantly shorter than the duration of the transmission period. A numerical study is also presented to validate the analytical framework and the results of our analysis, and a comparison is made of the throughput of the ALOHA, CSMA, and ideal scheduling methods in terms of data frame period, as well as time and frequency domains. This research provides a theoretical analysis of the performance of ALOHA and CSMA protocols in the presence of interference and possible solutions to the issues of interference and jamming in FMCW radar systems. It proposes a modified CSMA protocol to manage this interference more effectively and presents the results of a numerical study to validate the developed model. This study has implications for the design of radar systems that utilize time-domain processing methods and the development of radar systems that are more resistant to jamming. It demonstrates the need for further research into the development of efficient communication protocols for radar systems that utilize frequency modulation continuous wave technology. Through comprehensive experiments on various text datasets, the paper demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in single-model evaluations for both machine translation and summarization tasks, achieving improvements of up to +24.3 in BLEU scores. Furthermore, the paper explores the exploration of zero-shot learning applications for SparseGAN, showcasing its potential for handling out-of-domain data. The model's versatility is also highlighted through successful integration with a variety of activation functions and the sparsification technique being adaptable to multiple datasets. The paper provides in-depth architectural details and theoretical analyses of sparse gradients, along with a strong case for the sparseness of generative layers. The results of comprehensive experiments are also included in the paper, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The model's code has been made publicly available on GitHub, facilitating reproducibility of the findings. The paper's contributions are particularly significant for large-scale text generation tasks due to the significant improvements achieved with the proposed SparseGAN model. The former is crucial for understanding the compositionality of language, while the latter is essential for creating more engaging and versatile texts. The concept of spontaneous symmetry breaking is a fundamental phenomenon where an underlying continuous global symmetry is spontaneously disrupted at a physical level. This usually occurs when vacuum expectations are calculated for a theory that possesses the symmetry. A unique mechanism has been discovered, dubbed "triggered symmetry disruption," where the disruption of the symmetry is caused by a specific event, rather than a inherent feature of the vacuum. This process creates a cascade of symmetry disruptions, resulting in a more complex symmetry structure from a simpler original symmetry. Theoretical models, such as the Higgs-inflation model and certain scenarios of neutrino physics, can be understood through the lens of triggered symmetry disruption. The discovered mechanism advises physicists to examine the conditions that trigger symmetry disruptions, alongside the typical approach of calculating vacuum expectations. The interplay between triggered symmetry disruptions and the usual spontaneous symmetry disruption will be explored in the case of the Higgs-inflation model. The calculation of the potential for this model reveals that the inflationary sector causes a disruption of the electroweak symmetry, leading to an interesting connection between the mass scales of the heavy neutrons and the cosmological inflation. The article also discusses the experimental verification of the discovered symmetry disruptions in the case of the Higgs boson, specifically highlighting that the distribution of the hadronic decay products in the direction perpendicular to the beam line, known as $A_{\rm obs}$, will be the key for the investigation. The value of $A_{\rm obs}$ is expected to be very small, ranging from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$. The article also discusses the use of a leading-logarithm accuracy in the resummation of medium-induced parton branchings, resulting in an analytical estimate of $A_{\rm obs}$ in the limit of heavy quarks. This will provide the basis for a more sophisticated study of $A_{\rm obs}$ in the case of light quarks. The article is a follow-up to the published article arXiv:2103.02978 and a more comprehensive study of the triggered symmetry disruption chain in the context of heavy quark dynamics will be the subject of a forthcoming article. In fact, we are providing a more general framework that identifies the necessary and sufficient conditions for a family of independent, normally distributed matrices to exhibit the type B freeness property.
