Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, they still require extensive labeling. A key current research trend is domain adaptation, which enables the transfer of expertise from thoroughly labeled datasets to new datasets representing similar anatomical structures. To further enhance this process, our proposal introduces a novel technique for semi-supervised learning that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data. By employing a contrastive learning approach, our model adapts to new datasets with reduced labeling, thereby improving performance. A thorough evaluation of our method on realistic cardiac segmentation datasets demonstrates its superiority over non-domain adaptation baselines. Notably, our method achieves notable gains in adaptation efficiency, successful implementations of domain adaptation across new structures with limited or no labeled data, and a notable expansion of the capacity to adapt to novel datasets containing new anatomical structures with minimal or no labeled data. High-powered laser pulses can undergo a shift in their polarization as they interact with plasma over a significant distance. Research indicates that, under specific magnetized conditions, the polarization of these pulses can not only change but also amplify, showing an increase of up to three times the initial polarization amplitude. This phenomenon occurs due to the interaction of the laser with charged particles, particularly electrons, which become magnetized as the intensity of the laser reaches 1 times 10 to the power of 14 watts per square centimeter. This leads to a shift in the plasma's density, creating a gradient that causes a rotation in the laser's polarization over a distance of one meter. This rotation, achieved without the need for extra optical components, could be utilized for the purpose of optical vacuum polarization, thereby providing a marker for studying the propagation of high-powered laser pulses in diverse plasma environments. Furthermore, the potential existence of this phenomenon in magneto-static plasmas reduces the stringent density requirements, making it potentially applicable in simpler laboratory settings. Studies have also demonstrated that this phenomenon can occur in conjunction with the amplification of laser energy, a feature that could be leveraged to create novel methods of laser pulse shaping. A theoretical model, supported by the outcomes of supporting experiments, lays out the underlying mechanism that gives rise to this polarization alteration and amplification effect, thereby paving the way for the design of optimized experiments aimed at producing this phenomenon in a controlled environment. A further exploration of this phenomenon could disclose novel strategies for the creation of unique laser pulse shapes necessary in a variety of experimental applications. Lastly, a discussion is initiated on the possibility of achieving this phenomenon in a compact, noble gas jet-based target with consistent properties, a development that could lead to the wider availability of this phenomenon for utilization in high-tech experiments requiring the shaping of laser pulses. We calculated the electric dipole moment (EDM) of the tau lepton using perturbative QCD at next-to-leading order, taking into consideration the influence of heavier thighs larger than 1 GeV. In the charm quark mass range between 0.1 and 0.3 GeV, we calculated the EDM within the one-loop approximation, also considering the impact of heavier thighs larger than 1 GeV up to the next-to-leading order. Furthermore, we determined the EDM in the limit of heavy s quarks at next-to-leading order. In the mass range between 0.1 and 0.3 GeV for the s quark, we derived the EDM within the one-loop approximation, as well as at next-to-leading order for heavy s quarks. However, a significant obstacle to accurately measuring this parameter is the contamination from large-scale gradient fluctuations induced by cosmic structure formation. In order to achieve the desired precision on this parameter, it is essential to remove the lensing distortion induced by gravitational forces on the microwave background spectrum. This task is complicated because it requires removing a subtle signature from a noisy signal. It also offers better robustness to the assumption that the primordial fluctuations have a random Gaussian distribution, and therefore does not introduce new parameters to estimate. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established an intriguing connection between differential forms and the Pontrjagin classes, achieving this through the use of explicit, elementary calculations in the context of algebras. This relationship was notably shown to hold independently of the choice of differential form definition. Our aim is to present a detailed explanation of their method, followed by a demonstration of how this approach leads to a derivation of the classical Pontrjagin class properties. We also explore the potential implications of their technique on other characteristic classes, proposing a general framework based on their strategy. Furthermore, we investigate the compatibility of this approach with the geometric Berezkovski series and show that it aligns with the traditional differential geometric framework. Our findings suggest that the classical properties of the Pontrjagin classes can be derived solely from the algebraic properties of the differential forms, establishing an indirect connection between the geometric and algebraic descriptions of these classes. We also provide a discussion on the role of ambient algebras in maintaining the coherence of the differential forms and suggest that the choice of such an algebra is dictated by its fundamental properties. Building upon this understanding, we predict that the Pontrjagin classes will remain unchanged when shifting from one differential form set to another equivalent set, a hypothesis that we refer to as semi-invariance. We verify this property for the double covering and Frobenius functors. Notably, we discover that the Pontrjagin classes will not remain unchanged under the Golod-Shaferevich criterion, a finding that we prove through the examination of a specific example. Our findings lead us to a broader conjecture that connections between the geometric and algebraic descriptions of differential forms hold the key to understanding the behavior of the characteristic classes. We also explore the connections between the differential forms and the total Chern classes, hypothesizing that the latter may serve as a tool for further analysis of the characteristic classes in the context of algebras. SN~2020jfo, classified as a Type II with a short plateau duration, exhibited unusual characteristics in its light curves and spectra. During its initial plateau phase, SN~2020jfo's decline rate was abnormal, followed by a prolonged decline rate similar to that of other Type IIs. In spectra, a H-alphabalmer line with a distinctive double-peaked profile was observed, displaying a semi-empirical analysis similar to that of SNe with longer plateaus, although with some differences in ratio. A comparison with other Type IIs showed that SN~2020jfo's light curve and spectral features didn't match any other supernovae in our database, leading to difficulty in determining the progenitor's identity. A potential explosion energy or density variation or SN~2020jfo's unique pre-explosion environment could be responsible for its observed characteristics during expansion. A Type IIb supernova explosion energy variation could also explain the occurrence of SN~2020jfo, potentially linked to a similar event in the X-ray afterglow, along with a dark companion star that could provide clues on SN~2020jfo's progenitor identity. To study galaxy evolution, researchers utilize sub-halo structures and mass accretion history, which are often represented through a set of parameters that include mass, position, velocity, and other characteristics. While the mass and position parameters contribute significantly to determining a galaxy's mass, its velocity and orientation have a relatively minor effect on its mass assignment. Nonetheless, both effects become more pronounced when considering other galaxy properties such as star formation activity. Given the importance of these parameters in modeling galaxy evolution, it is essential to accurately determine the velocity field of galaxies. Unfortunately, current N-body simulations are not sufficiently detailed to capture the distribution of galaxies through their cosmic web structure. As a result, a deep learning-based model, referred to as HaloGAN, is developed to generate a galaxy's local velocity field based on its surrounding cosmic structure. By incorporating particle positions and local halo properties as input, HaloGAN produces both the linear and angular components of a galaxy's velocity vector. When compared to traditional mass conservation-based methods, HaloGAN demonstrates improved accuracy in mass preservation, mass conservation, and angular momentum preservation. Additionally, HaloGAN significantly reduces the number of necessary halo structure parameters, making it more computationally efficient. When integrating this model into galaxy evolution simulations, it is shown that both mass conservation-based methods and HaloGAN result in similar distribution functions for mass accretion rates and sub-halo masses. However, galaxies simulated with HaloGAN exhibit enhanced star formation rates and mass-to-light ratios due to improved mass assignment, leading to a more accurate modeling of galaxy evolution. Moreover, the developed model facilitates realistic simulation of multiple galaxy populations, enabling distinct populations to be accurately modeled without requiring separate initial conditions. Furthermore, the model demonstrates improved performance when integrating multiple galaxy interactions, resulting in enhanced understanding of galaxy evolution behavior, particularly regarding the formation of massive galaxies. The model is open-sourced and available for public use. A demonstration of its usability is provided in an accompanying Jupyter notebook available on GitHub. Additionally, the paper is accompanied by an open discussion on the arXiv forum. The developed model is executed on both local machines and remote clusters via Slurm. A tutorial on setting up the model on a remote cluster is available on GitHub. We present a novel numerical approach for generating equilibrium configurations of rotating stars in general relativity. This method utilizes a conservative and consistent formulation of the Einstein field equations, solving the relativistic hydrodynamics equations through iterative improvement. We have successfully developed a suite of libraries to efficiently compute the properties of rotating stars in both barotropic and stratum-specific cases, leveraging multiple roots of the relativistic rotational perturbation equations. Our method allows for rotations that produce both stable and unstable modes, and at various Roche lobe filling factors. We have validated our method against multiple benchmarks, and employ it to investigate the behavior of neutron stars and white dwarfs in rotation-driven evolution. Furthermore, we have explored the composition gradient of rotating stars, demonstrating that the barotropic approximation holds for moderate rotations, but significant non-barotropic structures form at high rotations. Our research provides a framework for the study of rotationally driven evolution in stars. Furthermore, we have constructed maps illustrating the behavior of rotating stars at different rotations and compositions, and have made significant advancements in the performance of our computational code, enhancing our capacity to simulate a wider range of star types. The adverse effects of social determinants on health have been thoroughly documented, yet their implementation in clinical settings remains limited due to difficulties in accessing relevant information. The present study proposes a data mining approach that utilizes a marker-driven method to identify social determinants of health within unstructured clinical notes. This approach was successfully applied to ICD codes that are associated with poor health outcomes following hospital discharge. The system we developed extracts 132 social determinants of health from electronic health records with an overall F-score of 0.81. This technique could potentially enhance the quality of transition care by providing healthcare professionals with accurate information on patients' living situations. To achieve this, our system would need to be integrated with existing health information systems, and further research is needed to explore its potential integration into clinical decision-support tools. This study is centered on a swimming mechanism known as the "scallop theorem," which states that certain rigid bodies with two degrees of freedom, like some swimmer models, can only change position by rotating around their center of mass. We aim to find the optimal trajectory for a swimmer of this type to travel between two points, as its movement is constrained by the scallop theorem's limitations. We will consider multiple scenarios to test this theory. First, we examine two-dimensional swimming without any obstructions. Then, we move on to the challenge of finding the optimal three-dimensional path, doing so under the constraint of not hitting any boundaries. Finally, we explore the best strategy for swimming in a two-dimensional space with boundaries, and all of these scenarios are represented mathematically in a generic form known as the scalar sub-Riemann problem. A key aspect of this research is the development of a method for breaking down these swimming pathways into individual components that can be analytically defined. We create a general formula for calculating the optimal three-dimensional swimming trajectory in the absence of boundary restrictions. Additionally, we establish the criteria for swimmers that will complete the task in equal time periods, effectively identifying all possible optimal solutions for swimming in three-dimensional space without boundary restrictions. We also demonstrate the criteria for swimmers that will complete the task in equal time periods for swimming in two-dimensional space with boundary restrictions. The COVID-19 pandemic brought about significant changes in human mobility and social interaction, with varying impacts on different socioeconomic groups. To examine the effects of pandemic period restrictions on urban interactions, our analysis of a mobility dataset from a major US city reveals how certain individual behaviors are linked to income levels. By comparing the pre-pandemic and pandemic period distributions of urban interaction behaviors, we identify a notable increase in income-based disparities during the pandemic, likely resulting from reduced social interactions outside of work. This research paper proposes a new concept called "Command Deciphering Code" (CDC) to ensure the security of nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA) communications between an allaying point and distant users who may be malicious. When the allaying point transmits messages to these users, they can decipher the coding used to combine messages for different individuals, thus compromising the security of the communication. A method was developed to differentiate between genuine and distant users based on the performance of conventional applications, and a code name "Deciphering Code of Distinction" (DCD) was created to securely communicate with users at these distances. However, this code is insecure to users closer to the allaying point. As a result, an alternative approach, known as CDC, was created to securely communicate with these close-minded users. The proposed CDC method enhances the security of these users without affecting the performance of conventional applications. Simulations were conducted to compare the new CDC method with the conventional DCD method, and the results showed that CDC achieves better performance than DCD. The poor performance of users subject to CDC/DCD codes is compensated with additional transmission signals. The code name DCD/CDC can be designed with existing tools and has straightforward implementation. Moreover, the proposed method integrates securely with 5G/6G CRAN systems. However, the introduction of dependent types in a constructive proof system introduces barbershop paradoxes and similar inconsistencies, which can lead to non-terminating computations during type checking. To address this issue, this paper proposes the concept of robust normalization for the Calculus of Constructions, a type theory that incorporates dependent types in a constructive proof system. The proposed normalization function is robust as it can handle a wide range of invalid and inconsistent types without entering into infinite computations during type checking. The development of robust normalization relies on the use of well-kinded terms, effectively preventing the emergence of non-terminating computations. The paper also explores the application of robust normalization to handling types with inconsistent inequalities, such as $forall x. x = \bot$. The proposed technique involves the conversion of such types into a consistent form, and the development of a proof that the converted types behave identically. The paper presents the details of robust normalization, including its implementation in the Coq proof assistant, and the results obtained using this technique. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of robust normalization in preventing non-terminating computations during type checking. Concurrent programming on GPUs is becoming increasingly popular due to their high performance potential.  However, achieving reliable and efficient concurrency on GPUs is complicated by their unique architecture, which includes a limited number of memory addresses that can be accessed simultaneously. The current memory allocation methods for GPUs are primarily based on first-come-first-served and batch allocation strategies but do not consider development needs such as inheritance and polymorphism. Our research presents a new object-oriented memory allocator called DynaSOAr, which is concurrent, efficient, and development-friendly for GPU programs. DynaSOAr uses a space array to manage memory and introduces an innovative "super-object" concept, allowing for the efficient allocation of derived classes that inherit from base classes. In experiments, DynaSOAr showed improved memory usage and reduced fragmentation compared to existing methods, and our code is available online for reference. In total, we incorporated 104 different memory allocation functions into our tests, using C++11 for compatibility. Our findings indicate that DynaSOAr's average memory fragmentation is 259KB, which is significantly lower than that of other methods with the highest fragmentation at 534KB for batch-based allocation. In addition, DynaSOAr's performance in solving the Jacobi method for matrix multiplication is up to 30% better than other methods, and our analysis of memory access patterns confirms that DynaSOAr's concurrent development supports low memory usage and reduced fragmentation. As a result, we believe that DynaSOAr will become an ideal choice for object-oriented GPU programming in the future. The complications of programming GPUs in an object-oriented way could be alleviated by introducing a new type of pointer called the "super-pointer", which can directly manage memory for derived classes, and our research shows that such an approach results in up to 5 times better performance and significantly lower memory fragmentation. In addition, the memory allocation method we developed is over 5 times more efficient than existing methods for large-scale memory allocations, and our experiments with a scientific computing application showed that it can complete tasks 10% faster and with much lower memory fragmentation. Therefore, we plan to release our compiler framework that supports the "super-pointer" data type and our proposed memory allocation method for the benefit of the research community, and we believe that such an approach will become an industry standard in the future. The structure of three-dimensional clouds has long been a topic of research, and recent studies suggest that certain clouds exhibit a veiled core phenomenon. This core, present at the center of thick cloud masses, forms when light from the cloud base is blocked by the cloud's depth, creating a layer where light cannot easily pass. As a result, this core region appears darker than its surrounding areas. To investigate this further, researchers used data from the MISR and MODIS satellite instruments, which offer simultaneous high-resolution imagery of clouds from space. By analyzing their data, they were able to identify the veiled core region within opaque cloud masses, providing a direct observation of cloud structure. From the reflectance differences between the core and surrounding areas, they were able to estimate the cloud optical depth, and subsequently, the cloud depth. Notably, the cloud depths derived from this method matched previous measurements, and the analysis indicated that the core region is typically located within 20% of the total cloud depth. This discovery provides a direct measurement of cloud structure and can be incorporated into models of cloud optical properties. Additionally, it highlights the capability of space-based cloud imaging, combined with the angular resolution of MISR, as a powerful tool for investigating the three-dimensional aspects of clouds. By using this technique, researchers can study the relationships between cloud structure and other factors such as weather patterns and aerosol presence. A numerical model is developed to analyze this propulsion mechanism, yielding results indicating that it is possible to achieve specific impulses greater than 50,000 seconds using a 100 kilowatt system with a 10 percent efficiency rate. This assessment focuses on the 'translucency' phase alone, without considering the entire life cycle of the propellant ions. A simplified theory is also presented to explain the translucency phenomenon, suggesting that it results from a highly transparent state of the plasma during the critical phase. This theory predicts that the phase duration is directly proportional to the square of the laser intensity and the charge state of the ions, providing a basis for the design of optimal propulsion systems. A 10 megawatt system is calculated to achieve a 90 kilogram-force thrust with a 20 micro-meter grain size, while a 100 kilowatt system produces a 9 gram-force thrust with a 1 micro-meter grain size. These findings indicate that this propulsion approach has the potential to achieve high specific impulses efficiently. This research is a fundamental step in the scientific investigation of this propulsion mechanism, and it is hoped that it will pave the way for a more in-depth analysis of this novel and promising technology. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced in high-energy electron-photon interactions, specifically through the process of pair production in intense laser-matter interactions.  However, due to limitations in current positron detection systems, research in this area has been restricted to long-term, low-intensity production methods.  Recent advancements in laser technology and detection systems capabilities have created opportunities to explore more prolific, polarization-sensitive production methods.  Using multi-dimensional simulation models, we found that positrons with over 1000 times background rate and 1% polarization level can be achieved with modern detection systems, especially under conditions of intense laser interactions with thin targets and in situations where the produced photons are polarized and have sufficient energy to overcome positron production restrictions.  A discussion on the physical parameters that affect production rates and polarization levels is presented, in addition to an analysis of the optimal conditions required to achieve the desired positron properties.  Furthermore, we explore the possibility of achieving dense, polarizationized positron sources that could have implications for particle physics research, such as potential uses in laser-proton accelerators and in research involving large magnetic spectrometers.  A case is made for the construction of a sophisticated detection system capable of accurately measuring the properties of positrons produced through laser-matter interactions.  Consideration should be given to funding such a project with resources available through the development of new detection technologies.  In conclusion, our research uncovers novel information on the production of polarized positrons and we hope this study serves as a starting point for discussions on the development of new detection technologies and potential uses for polarized positrons.  Further research is needed to fully understand the potential benefits of polarized positrons produced through laser-matter interactions and we anticipate that our study will contribute meaningfully to these efforts.  In the process, we may witness breakthroughs in our understanding of the interaction between high-energy electrons and intense photon fields.  As a result, we could see the development of new methods for producing polarized electrons, a fundamental component used in particle accelerator experiments, such as those involving the investigation of rare photon decays from heavy mesons.  In the end, our research may pave the way for the creation of new sources of polarized, dense positrons that could have far-reaching implications for particle physics research.  As we consider new funding opportunities for the development of detection technologies, we should also contemplate supporting projects that could yield novel sources of polarized, dense positrons.  By doing so, we may unlock new possibilities for particle physics research

Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries. Furthermore, we established a theoretical expression predicting stability based on magnetic Rossby number and confirmed our prediction with multiple tests, paving the way for simplified stability criteria in future studies. Additionally, we explored potential instability developments in both locally weak and strong modes within stable, non-turbulent stellar interiors. Our findings provide a framework for interpreting magnetic field data in stars where the interior structure is known. In reverse, our results also outline a means by which the stellar interior structure can be inferred from observed stable magnetic field patterns. Last, we experimented with conducting a stability analysis using actual stellar models, replicating the stable configurations found in our prior simulations, and verified that these stable configurations persist in realistic stellar environments. In the process, we established a method for defining the stability of a magnetic field within any given region of a stable, non-turbulent stellar interior utilizing the magnetic Rossby number. This approach is not only applicable to axisymmetric configurations but also provides a means by which the full three-dimensional magnetic field energy distribution can be compared to the criteria necessary for stability in the most susceptible, locally weak modes. Ultimately, our research provides a foundation for investigating the interaction between stable stellar interiors and the long-lasting magnetic fields found in such environments. Using the functional renormalization group formalism, we develop a strategy to solve approximate flow equations in quantum field theories. We leverage this approach to examine a one-dimensional $O(N)$ symmetric model, as the simplicity of this model allows us to numerically solve the flow equations without approximation. By comparing the solutions to the flow equations with the exact results for the one-dimensional $O(N)$ model, we establish a framework for assessing the accuracy of approximate solutions in the presence of approximations such as truncations of the derivative expansion. Furthermore, we investigate how the degree of approximation affects the convergence of the solution, and we explore the precision of the approximate solutions for a range of physical parameters. As the renormalization group flows in fractal dimensions pose significant computational challenges for our numerical methods, we restrict our computations to parameter values in the range $0\leq z\leq1.5$. Additionally, we find that even in cases where the approximate solutions yield reliable numerical data, the precision can drop to as low as $10^{-2}$ when we reach the upper limit of this range. Nonetheless, our analysis suggests that for values of $z$ below $1$, the precision is consistently better than $10^{-3}$. Furthermore, we find no significant bias in our error estimates. Building on our testing protocol, in a forthcoming paper we will apply this framework to examine a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator with a $N$-component scalar field. This model serves as a prototype for a broader class of regularizable quantum field theory models. Additionally, we will investigate the renormalization group flow in $1+d$ dimensions, where $d$ is the fractal dimension, for this harmonic oscillator model. This will involve a detailed analysis of how the approximate solutions for the flow equations relate to the exact results for the one-dimensional $O(N)$ model, including a thorough examination of how the degree of approximation affects the convergence of the solution for this broader class of models. This testing protocol will enable us to assess the precision of our approximate solutions in the presence of approximations such as truncations of the derivative expansion across a wide range of physical parameters. This will allow us to evaluate the accuracy of this approach for solving approximate flow equations in quantum field theories. This evaluation will, in turn, facilitate a comprehensive comparison with alternative methods for solving approximate flow equations, such as approximate renormalization group and lattice Monte Carlo simulations. This comparison will provide a framework for identifying the limitations and potential biases of this approach, as well as its strengths and weaknesses

Music theory lessons are often complicated to manage due to their diverse nature.
A key element of music theory is chord progressions, which are used in this paper
as a basic construct for education.
A novel approach called Meta-Inquiry is introduced, which utilizes logical
rules to generate engaging music theory questions.
These questions are created through a set of logical operations that both
identify essential characteristics of music and are easily solvable when answered
with a specific chord progression.
The Meta-Inquiry approach is applied to developing questions about
coherence, succession, and parallelism in music, which are subsequently
combined into complete lessons with the aid of sequence-to-sequence models.
The results show that students learn chord progressions more effectively when
presented with these generated questions compared to traditional approaches.
The code for the music question generation model has been made publicly available
on GitHub, which also includes an user interface for creating custom lessons. 
This model has also been deployed as a user-friendly web application called
Pied Piper, which allows users to create custom music lessons for sale on Udemy. 
However, Udemy's policies do not permit the use of automated assessment tools
in paid courses, which has resulted in the application being taken off the platform. 
UDACITY has expressed interest in Pied Piper as a potential tool for their courses. 
A similar application called Harmonize has also been developed for solo practice. 
Both of these applications have been demonstrated to be more engaging and just as
effective as traditional methods for teaching music theory. 
A video demonstrating the applications' functionality is available with the code. 
A udio lessons created with this technology have been released on Spotify and Google Music. 
A Udemy course created with this technology remains available for paid instruction.

A key aspect of massive star formation is the core collapse model, which emphasizes the significance of quiescent core development. To shed light on this process, we examined the Dragon infrared dark nebula using simulations, observing how a dense core formed within this nebula. The core showed characteristics similar to those found in fly-through observations of the B68 nebula, and it exhibited a temperature around 10 K, with a density two orders of magnitude higher than its surrounding environment. The core's dimensions are approximately 3.8 pc in length, 1.4 pc in width, and it weighs around 1.6 x 10 to the power of 3 solar masses. Our simulations indicated that the core's formation took around 5 to 6 million years and that it's now in the stage where core collapse can occur. Additionally, we found evidence of a highly unstable core within a 0.14 pc-wide central region, which may eventually break into smaller fragments that could become massive protostars. The time it takes for these fragments to collapse into protostars ranges from 0.5 to 2.5 million years, depending on the mass of each fragment. Our research provides clear visual evidence of a quiescent core developing within the Dragon nebula, offering a hopeful sign that this process could lead to the formation of massive stars. We developed and tested an multifaceted measure of curiosity based on these factors and used it to explore how primary school pupils learn in a real-world, small-group science learning environment that is supported by advanced technologies. We validated our theory with video recordings of the pupils and found that they exhibit different types of curiosity such as exploratory, confirmatory, and frustration-induced curiosity. We believe that our approach will be useful for tracking the level of curiosity in real-world learning environments and in designing more engaging, effective learning experiences that are tailored to the needs and interests of individual pupils.  Our investigation will also be useful for any domain that relies on complex systems behaving effectively, such as economic systems, political systems, and organizational systems. The creation of efficient urban traffic networks relies heavily on the integration of road infrastructure and vehicle dynamics. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, but our investigation reveals a critical flaw in these models. We demonstrate that due to their complex architecture, these models can exhibit two undesirable properties: 1) overresponse and 2) overstability. Our research indicates that the former arises from the tendency of neural networks to favor simplicity, and the latter from the difficulty of adequately assessing the reliability of these models. The outcomes of our studies show that score stability varies significantly across topics, with scores for stemming topics (such as description and narrative) being much more consistent than scores for growing topics (such as argumentation and persuasion). Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the intrinsic nature of these topics, rather than the scoring models used, is the primary factor influencing the variability observed in our results. As a result, the evaluations and rankings produced by these models are untrustworthy. To address this issue, we propose a multi-faceted framework that incorporates both score stability and responsiveness in addition to existing validity metrics. Our framework serves as a critical component in the development of robust automated scoring models. To create this framework, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the contexts and considered expert opinions to establish a set of criteria that can effectively evaluate the validity, reliability, and utility of automated scoring models. Moreover, we applied our proposed framework to a comprehensive essay dataset to demonstrate its practical utility. The criteria we established can be used to assess the performance of different automated scoring models, and our methodology for evaluating the outcomes is fully transparent and easily replicable. Our research has significant implications for the development of high-quality automated scoring models, and we hope that our proposed framework will be widely adopted to ensure the reliability and validity of these models. A key aspect of our framework is a systematic approach to evaluating the validity, reliability, and utility of automated scoring models, and we believe that this methodology can also be useful for developing other contextual evaluation tools, such as automated speech analysis tools. Additionally, our results have important implications for the development of advanced neural network architectures, such as transformer models, and we hope that our research will contribute positively to these efforts. We investigate the Ramsey property for V-shaped posets within Boolean algebras, exploring their behavior and determining the associated Ramsey values. Our findings are particularly notable in relation to the cyclic posets, where we establish a link between the Boolean algebra Ramsey property and the cyclic poset Ramsey property. Our results also consider the impact of the Duplicity Principle on Boolean algebra Ramsey theory, especially regarding the ultimate Ramsey type behavior of structures like the finite antichains and the single-element posets. We are also proactive in providing a publicly accessible database for the Boolean algebra Ramsey values, available at the website 'Boolean Ramseys'. Finally, we conclude by highlighting some intriguing open questions and potential areas for further exploration in this field. We include a appendix for handling comments and providing a clear explanation of the terminology used in this research for the benefit of the reader.

Current dialogue comprehension models are typically large and costly to fine-tune on numerous tasks. A potential solution involves pre-training dialogue models using contrastive learning, given the vast amounts of unlabeled dialogue data available. To build upon existing two-tier models, we propose a tree-structured approach that combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training. In this approach, a pre-finetuned backbone network represents dialogue contexts as compact, task-specific vectors. A task-agnostic matcher then uses these representations to learn dialogue context representations in an unsupervised manner during the semi-supervised contrastive pre-training process. This matcher is incorporated into a tree-like schedule to efficiently utilize limited labeled data. Our evaluation shows that our method effectively enables few-shot cross-domain dialogue comprehension. Notably, our results indicate that pre-finetuning the backbone network on a small labeled dataset significantly improves performance in the target tasks during the semi-supervised contrastive pre-training process. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/THU-DCL/S2CPT. Our model achieved the leading score in the DialoGLUE evaluation challenge at https://www.dialoglue.org/leaderboards/xfds/1/. Our approach also performed best in the 2022 Easy DialoGLUE subchallenge for single-shot dialogue comprehension. Our model's performance on certain easier tasks even approached human-level performance. However, it struggled with some zero-shot and single-shot target tasks during the DialoGLUE evaluation. Our analysis of these difficulties led us to further improve our method by adding a dialogue-specific matcher to obtain better performance in zero-shot and single-shot target tasks. With these enhancements, our method moved to the top position in the easy and total DialoGLUE leaderboards at https://www.dialoglue.org/leaderboards/xfds/2/. Our revised method's performance on certain zero-shot and single-shot target tasks also closed the gap with human-level performance. Our code and data for the revised method are also publicly available at https://github.com/THU-DCL/S2CPT. Multi-task reinforcement learning draws significant attention for its potential to resolve complex problems by breaking them down into various tasks. However, learning multiple tasks simultaneously is challenging due to destructive interference, which hinders the development of skilled behavior. To overcome this issue, we introduce a novel modular approach called MBMT, where each task is learned using a separate world model and the policies are shared across tasks. This approach reduces interference by segregating task representations, and we prove theoretically that it minimizes the interference term in the multi-task reinforcement learning objective. Our experiments demonstrate the advantages of MBMT to be robust to overfitting, significantly faster to train, and as effective as non-modular methods in solving complex navigation and control tasks. Moreover, MBMT scales efficiently to multiple tasks and learns a high level of generalization in each component, including the world model and policy networks. Our results indicate that MBMT achieves high performance on benchmark datasets by significantly outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods like REWIL and MTQ-learning. The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/UMI-CompInt/MBMT. Our primary auditory localization method is based on interaural intensity differences, which are straightforward to calculate, especially for mid-frequency sounds. In contrast, localizing sounds with minimal intensity differences, often present in background noise, relies heavily on time-difference analysis between the sound's arrival at each ear and is therefore more complicated to estimate. This task is further impeded by the absence of reliable afferent signals in such situations. Notably, head-related transfer functions, crucial for auditory localization, are difficult to pinpoint accurately in just the time and scatter domains for these difficult-to-localize sounds. This is illustrated by the significant discrepancy between predicted and actual auditory localization behavior as shown in our findings. These outcomes have significant implications for sound localization research, particularly in understanding how auditory localization is managed in noise, and for the development of more realistic audio simulation tools. In addition, these outcomes may be applied to improve the accuracy of bilateral cochlear implant users in localizing sounds. In our paper, we investigate these findings in some depth and offer several practical applications for which the data collected is also relevant. In our experiments, we used recordings from 20 normal hearing subjects to an audio source that could not be localized based on differences in sound intensity between the two ears. We then compared the subjects' actual responses with their perceptions, and also examined the head-related transfer functions of the difficult-to-localize sounds through analysis of the time and scatter domains. Our results showed a clear discrepancy between the actual responses and the predicted responses, and also highlighted the difficulties in pinpointing the head-related transfer functions in just the time and scatter domains for these difficult-to-localize sounds. Our findings in this rating task were supported by further evidence from additional listeners. We used these findings to re-examine the difficult-to-localize sounds in noise from a new methodological perspective, and based on our discussions, we believe that our study could also be relevant to the development of more accurate audio simulation tools. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have excelled in various social and infrastructure graph applications but often struggle with biomedical graph challenges due to data sparsity. Current distance-based GNNs models can lead to inaccurate results as they may propagate errors along graph paths. To resolve this issue, we introduce a new distance metric called the Lorentzian distance that considers a node's ego-features and its nearest neighbors. This distance metric forms a minimum spanning tree in a graph, thereby providing a unique path between any two nodes. We propose a novel Lorentzian GNN (LGN) model that leverages this distance metric, utilizing the minimum spanning tree structure to aggregate node representations. The LGN model significantly outperforms existing GNN models on various biomedical datasets in terms of prediction accuracy. Furthermore, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on certain benchmark tasks while being computationally efficient. We also introduce an end-to-end LGN model called Reentrant LGN (R-LGN) that matches the performance of traditional methods on certain classification tasks, while being highly efficient in terms of model parameters. A crucial aspect of our R-LGN model is its ability to attach meaningful node labels during the reentrant encoding process, thereby providing an interpretable model. Our model is open-sourced and is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/ssecaruso/Lorentzian-GNN. This work is a part of the Ph.D. thesis of the primary author, who is currently working on expanding this research in his postdoctoral studies. This paper is a revised and expanded version of our previous workshop paper presented at ICLR 2020, where it received the outstanding paper award. Our results demonstrate the LGN model's superiority over standard GNN models, while our theoretical analysis provides a rigorous background on this novel distance metric. Our experimentations are thorough, comprehensive, and report our original research findings, while our code is publicly available, enabling replication of our research findings. This study is a groundbreaking research in the field of graph neural networks, especially in the domain of bioinformatics, and our code and techniques will drive the development of innovative graph learning methods. Language barriers still significantly impede global progress, and existing translation methods primarily address written text. Speech translation has seen significant advancements but is currently limited to languages that share physical proximity, largely neglecting many vital dialects. A novel approach, called zero-shot voice translation, is introduced, allowing for the translation of spoken words into any language, including those previously unaffected by speech translation technologies. This goal is achieved by modifying speech-to-text and text-to-speech models to produce high-fidelity audio from unknown languages, thereby enabling seamless voice translation across language boundaries. Our proposed framework showcases exceptional performance on unseen languages in comparison to conventional speech translation systems, as evident from our results featuring MUSAN data and additional dialects in Arabic, Hindi, and Spanish. Furthermore, our model's capacity to handle challenging dialect translations is also illustrated through additional experiments. Our code is readily available online for reproduction of our findings. As speech translation continues to gain momentum, the field is on the cusp of a breakthrough in zero-shot voice translation, presenting numerous opportunities and paving the way for innovative applications and breakthroughs. As we venture further into the era of artificial intelligence, the ability to translate spoken words into any language will become an essential capability, and our proposed approach is a significant step in this direction. Merging speech and natural language processing is crucial for realizing this vision, and our proposed framework is a landmark achievement in this convergence of technologies. As we look to the future, our focus will be on refining the phonetic information generated by text-to-speech models, ensuring that the speech-to-speech models are highly adaptable, and exploring alternative methods for zero-shot speech synthesis. Moreover, our work is an invitation to the broader speech and NLP communities to participate in DataILS, a leading dataset creation initiative that is instrumental in developing high-quality dialect datasets via crowdsourcing. This dataset plays a critical role in the development of our state-of-the-art zero-shot voice translation technology, and we hope that our results will motivate more researchers to engage with DataILS and contribute to the advancement of speech translation in low-resource languages and dialects. This work is a significant milestone in the convergence of speech and NLP, two technologies that are now merging into a unified discipline called speech-NLP. This new field is characterized by the overlap of previous technology boundaries, such as the distinction between speech and NLP, and our work is a prime example of this convergence, as we refer to it. Using deep learning, automatic image analysis can accurately detect diseases from radiological images, such as chest X-rays, with high success rates. A notable example is the detection of COVID-19 pneumonia. However, there is a growing ethical concern about modifying medical images for purposes other than medical treatment, given that these images contain sensitive information about a person's health. In the context of chest X-rays, this issue is particularly pressing due to the high frequency of abnormal findings, which poses a continuous risk to patients' health even after initial diagnosis. This research aims to break new ground in the field by exploring methods to modify medical images in a way that takes into consideration the patient's health status. To achieve this, we developed a system that combines a health risk model and a generative model to ensure that modified images meet certain safety criteria. This system was specifically designed to handle chest X-rays and address health-related concerns. For evaluation purposes, we created a unique dataset that includes a variety of medical conditions as well as health risk factors. Our results show that our approach is effective in detecting both primary and secondary diseases from modified images, which would not be possible with conventional image-to-image translation methods. Furthermore, our empirical studies highlighted the significance of disease codes in medical imaging, a finding that we believe will be valuable to the broader research community. Our project's primary contribution is its exploration of the new concept of illness-aware image-to-image translation, which we believe has vast potential for exploration. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization. It enables the creation of various non-linear visual representations, such as U-matrices, density plots, and interactive 3D embeddings, allowing for simultaneous visualization of data points and corresponding feature values. The tool also facilitates the generation of intrinsic dimensionality plots, ascending/descending order checks for data coordinates, and simultaneous 3D data point and feature visualizations through Jmol integration. ViDaExpert supports learning outcomes assessment and offers an easy-to-use interface for importing data, selecting dimensionality reduction algorithms, and customizing visual representations. It is designed for educational purposes to introduce students to nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques like Isomap, Local Linear Embedding, and Uniform Manifold Approximation, and to promote critical thinking about data visualization reliability. ViDaExpert is written in Python with RPyMCA used for Java Jmol integration, and is compatible with recent Windows, macOS, and Linux operating systems. We develop a method to approximate the Laplace operator under Newtonian potentials over flat domains using a limited number of boundary points. This involves utilizing a collection of centers to split the domain into spatial regions, which allows for the application of the Kirchhoff transformation to compute a harmonic volume related to the original function. This computational method can be efficiently optimized with an interior point-corrector technique. Furthermore, we derive an error bound that determines when the approximation can yield a difference of up to an arbitrary small amount with the original function. This leads to an algorithm to compute an approximation of a Helmholtz equation with a Newtonian potential on flat domains. We support our method with numerical examples showcasing its performance. 

In dynamic scenarios, we extend this method to the time-dependent Helmholtz equation with a Newtonian potential. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method over domains with changing boundaries and provide a preliminary analysis of its behavior. This method holds promise for swift assessments of Newtonian potentials in scenarios involving the transportation of passive substances in fluid dynamics.
